chapter_note: This chapter is predominantly institutional/editorial material explaining the cosmic significance of Manichaean liturgical practices (assent and amen). The substrate core is limited to ¶2-4: a compact teaching that maps assent→summons and amen→obedience (answer), then describes how these cosmic entities functioned as portals for the First Man's redemption and as purifiers of the living soul. From ¶5 onward, the teaching applies these cosmic archetypes to congregational worship practice — describing liturgical sealing, the formation of ascending images from collective sound, healing power, and overcoming temptation. All of this later material has one side of its mapping reaching into institutional practice ('the congregation', 'great crowds of people', 'the elect', 'their alms'). The text is heavily damaged throughout with extensive lacunae, especially ¶4 and ¶10-16. Substrate vocabulary is entirely concentrated in the first half (8.71→0.00), confirming the core teaching ends early. Gardner notes this chapter was completed from Funk's working text beyond the published edition.

paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue frame formula ('Once again, one of the disciples [...] to him: Tell me, my master') and liturgical-practice framing ('the name that we may utter over the blessing [...] we bless, and also the prayer by which we pray. Tell us:'). Retained the substantive cosmological question that defines the teaching topic.
paragraphs.temporal_note: The question 'What is the assent and the amen?' is substantive — it asks about the cosmic NATURE of these entities, and the answer (¶2-3) maps them to cosmic archetypes. The surrounding material about blessing and prayer is institutional context. Institutional score 4.55 confirms liturgical vocabulary.

paragraphs.core_text: The assent and the amen have come about from these great ones of the powers. They were given the name as the assent belongs to the summons and the amen belongs to the answer.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue frame attribution 'Our enlightener says to him:' — standard frame formula (dialogue_frame score 10.26).
paragraphs.temporal_note: This is the key correspondential mapping: assent→summons, amen→answer (obedience). Both sides stay within the cosmic system — liturgical terms mapped to cosmic entities. This establishes the archetype that the rest of the chapter will apply.

paragraphs.core_text: Just as the summons and the obedience are the ones that opened the portals of mercy and entreaty for the First Man, so they also became portals for the Mother of Life and the Father of the living. The First Man sought and found his redeemer. And also the Mother of Life and the Father of the living sought [...] this runner, who came forth from them, who is the First Man; but the summons and the obedience became the portals for them.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Pure substrate. Highest substrate score in the chapter (26.51). Describes cosmic process: summons/obedience as portals enabling the First Man's redemption. All entities (First Man, Mother of Life, Father of the living) and functions (portals, seeking, finding, redemption) are within the cosmic system. 'Runner' (the First Man) is a cosmological designation. No audience address, no institutional reference.

paragraphs.core_text: they have become portals for the aeons of greatness towards the First Man, and the soul that was conjoined with death. They became helpers [...] of the First Man during his ascent. They gave him [...] the Father of Life and the Mother of Life [...]. They are purifiers of the living soul, being helpers and bestowers of remembrance for it, be it either in [...] in the tree or in the creation of flesh [...]
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed 'Now, in this way' bridge connective at opening, and the fragmentary institutional extension: 'the holy church [...] the earth [...] summons and the obedience that [...] the portals [...] in the holy church [...] helpers, bestowers of power and collectors [...] teacher [...] purified for their sake [...].' The repeated references to 'the holy church' and 'teacher' mark the editorial extension where cosmic archetype is applied to the community. The boundary is uncertain due to extensive lacunae.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Mixed paragraph with clear substrate in the first portion (substrate 19.83, institutional 10.34). The cosmic teaching — portals for the aeons, helpers during the First Man's ascent, purifiers of the living soul — continues ¶3's cosmological narrative. 'The soul that was conjoined with death' is substrate soul-body binding language. The transition to 'the holy church' is the editorial seam where the cosmic archetype is applied to the institutional present.

Liturgical practice instruction: describes what happens when one blesses and responds with assent/amen ('shall seal the blesser'). One side of the mapping reaches into communal worship. Institutional score 4.44. Note the page marker ⟨p.292⟩ appears here but the chapter opened at ⟨p.291⟩ and ¶4 was ⟨p.293⟩ — possible folio displacement in the manuscript.

Highest institutional score in the chapter (18.18). Describes congregational liturgical practice: 'when the congregation will beseech an entreaty with a question, and they all answer and say verily and amen.' One side of every mapping reaches into communal worship ('the congregation', 'they all answer'). Clearly institutional.

Pedagogical formula 'Happen you know that' (appears also in ¶9) introduces teaching about assent/amen as 'a great person.' While the personification has cosmological resonance ('new birth daily, very good and honoured in the presence of the living ones above'), the entire passage is framed as audience address ('all of you', 'you rejoice', 'came to you profitably') explaining what the community's liturgical practice produces. The cosmic effect is triggered by institutional practice. Dialogue_frame score 6.67 reflects the pedagogical address.

Describes how collective liturgical sound forms a beautiful image that ascends to 'the land of tranquillity and peace.' The cosmic process (sound → collection → sculpting → image → ascent) is genuinely interesting cosmologically, and 'land of tranquillity and peace' is cosmic geography. However, the process is explicitly triggered by communal practice ('great crowds of people utter the assent and the amen') and concludes with 'their joy and their alms' — institutional vocabulary. One side reaches into congregational practice. Institutional score 3.09.

Opens third section per Gardner synopsis: assent/amen as 'a great power' for healing. 'Happen you know that' pedagogical formula (cf. ¶7). Describes praying over the sick — clearly institutional/pastoral application of cosmic power to community practice. Heavily damaged with many lacunae.
Very fragmentary (17 words). Continues healing theme: 'a great help comes to him from the assent and the amen.' Pastoral application.

Describes overcoming temptation through liturgical invocation: confession of sin, beseeching charity, calling assent/amen to annul 'the lust and the temptation.' References 'the elect' (institutional score 2.17). The power described operates through institutional practice (confession, communal prayer). Pastoral/institutional.
Continues prayer-over-person theme: 'a great power come to him out from the assent and the amen. It helps him.' Liturgical/pastoral application. Institutional score 4.35.

Very fragmentary (29 words). 'The assent and the amen go up to the ships' — references cosmic geography (ships of light), but in context of liturgical efficacy. The cosmic element is the destination of the liturgical act, not an independent cosmological mapping.

Extremely fragmentary (86 words but heavily lacunose). References 'the heavens and the ships' (cosmic geography) and 'the assent and the amen.' Seems to describe salvation/deliverance through liturgical invocation ('He is saved', 'they called over him'). Too fragmentary for confident classification but consistent with institutional/pastoral pattern of preceding paragraphs.

Very fragmentary (19 words). 'Behold' and 'your own cry' suggest direct address. Continues discussion of assent/amen. Too fragmentary for confident classification; classified as institutional consistent with surrounding context.

References 'the apostles, the first fathers' — institutional succession language. 'It might be uttered from God' and naming from apostles grounds the assent/amen in institutional authority. Fragmentary but clearly institutional.
Closing formula: 'Then, when the father [...] like this, he glorified and he [...].' Standard chapter-closing dialogue frame. 'The father' = editorial honorific for Mani. Very fragmentary (12 words).
